guide.title: Rugby, Brooklyn: An 1890s Name on Utica Avenue
guide.intro: Developers chose the name Rugby in the 1890s for what is now the eastern section of East Flatbush. Building accelerated after 1892, when they acquired roughly 65 acres expecting a promised subway extension, and again once the IRT line reached Nostrand Avenue in 1912 and the area grew quickly as a residential neighborhood. Before either, in May 1900, the Brooklyn Heights Railroad extended its Reid Avenue trolley line south along Utica Avenue to reach Rugby, terminating at Utica and Church Avenues: a streetcar suburb before any subway. The Remsen name that displaced it comes from the family of Joris Remsen, an early settler and landowner, and everyday and real-estate use shifted to Remsen Village from the mid-1990s.

sections.heading: What survives of the name
sections.body:
Rugby is a name more than a place with edges. Sources use Rugby and Remsen Village inconsistently for the same or overlapping ground: one passage calls it the eastern section of East Flatbush, another, citing 2020 Census tabulation areas, places Rugby north of Farragut, and press coverage sometimes hyphenates the two as Rugby-Remsen Village. No source gives a single definitive line, and none is asserted here. What the research does anchor is Utica Avenue, Rutland Road and the East 90s, with East 98th Street described in most sourced boundary descriptions as the eastern edge.

The Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue opened in 1957. It closed in 2017 for a renovation whose budget grew from an original $1 million to $10.2 million, delayed by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic, with a mobile library trailer serving patrons in the meantime. It reopened on a Monday in July 2021 with new heating and cooling, accessibility upgrades, a garden, a mural by the artist J. Mikal Davis and sustainable materials including cork and bamboo flooring. Kennedy King Playground, between Lenox Road and Clarkson Avenue, has been city parkland since October 1957, the same year the branch opened.

The eating on these blocks is Caribbean. Tasty Caribbean at 856 Utica Avenue and the Golden Krust Caribbean Bakery and Grill at 872 sit in a run of Caribbean-owned food businesses between roughly 850 and 960 Utica Avenue; Souljah, at 875 Rutland Road, is one of about a dozen Caribbean, Chinese and fast-food storefronts along the strip that runs out to the Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road station. All three were located through the city's restaurant-inspection records rather than press coverage, and each held an A grade at its most recent inspection.

By 2020 Census tabulation-area data, the Rugby area had between 30,000 and 39,999 Black residents, with the Hispanic, White and Asian populations each fewer than 5,000. The stretch of Church Avenue between Remsen Avenue and East 98th Street, co-named Bob Marley Boulevard in summer 2006, is covered on the Remsen Village page.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road, on the IRT New Lots Line, sits at the meeting of Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, on the border of East Flatbush and Brownsville; sources commonly describe East 98th Street as Rugby's eastern edge. It is served by the 3 at all times except late nights, when the 4 takes over, with extra 2 and 5 service at rush hours.

The IRT Nostrand Avenue Line stations sit near the western border of East Flatbush, on the opposite side from Rugby's East 98th Street edge, and are not a realistic access point here. That leaves the bus for the Utica Avenue side, where the library and both of its neighbouring kitchens stand. The B46 and B46 Select Bus Service run north-south along Utica Avenue, passing the Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue, and the corridor has carried this ground since the trolley line was extended here in 1900.

faq.question: How do I get to Rugby?
faq.answer: Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road on the IRT New Lots Line, at Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, is the station at the eastern edge; it is served by the 3, with the 4 taking over late nights and extra 2 and 5 service at rush hours. For the Utica Avenue side, the B46 and B46 Select Bus Service run past the Rugby branch library.

faq.question: Is Rugby the same place as Remsen Village?
faq.answer: Sources use the two names for the same or overlapping ground. Rugby was chosen by developers in the 1890s; Remsen Village came into everyday and real-estate use from the mid-1990s, and press coverage sometimes hyphenates them as Rugby-Remsen Village. No source draws a definitive line between them.

faq.question: Is the Rugby branch library open?
faq.answer: Yes. It closed in 2017 for a renovation that grew from a $1 million budget to $10.2 million and was held up by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic. It reopened on a Monday in July 2021; the source that reported the reopening does not print the calendar date, so none is given here.

places.name: Rugby Branch, Brooklyn Public Library
places.summary: The branch opened in 1957 and is named for Rugby, the 1890s developer name for this section of East Flatbush. It closed in 2017 for renovation and reopened on a Monday in July 2021.
places.history: The renovation grew from an original $1 million budget to $10.2 million, delayed by funding gaps, Hurricane Sandy repairs, contracting problems and the pandemic; a mobile library trailer served patrons during the closure. The reopened branch has new heating and cooling, accessibility upgrades, a garden, a mural by the artist J. Mikal Davis, and cork and bamboo flooring.

places.name: Kennedy King Playground
places.summary: A 0.79-acre NYC Parks playground running East 93rd to East 94th Street between Lenox Road and Clarkson Avenue.
places.history: NYC Parks acquired the site on October 24, 1957, the same year the Rugby branch library opened on Utica Avenue. It falls within Community District 17; Wikipedia's account of Brooklyn Community Board 17 lists Rugby among the district's neighborhoods and gives East 98th Street as the district's eastern boundary.

places.name: Tasty Caribbean
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant on Utica Avenue, part of a run of Caribbean-owned food businesses between roughly 850 and 960 Utica Avenue, near the Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on October 20, 2025.

places.name: Golden Krust Caribbean Bakery and Grill
places.summary: A Caribbean bakery and grill, an outlet of the Golden Krust chain, a few blocks from the Rugby branch library at 1000 Utica Avenue. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on June 2, 2026.

places.name: Souljah
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant on Rutland Road, among roughly a dozen Caribbean, Chinese and fast-food storefronts along this stretch near the Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road subway station. It was graded A at its most recent city health inspection, on February 9, 2026.

entries.name: Rugby Branch, Brooklyn Public Library

links.note: Rugby is the original name for the eastern section of East Flatbush, chosen by developers in the 1890s.
The B44 runs mostly along Nostrand Avenue through Crown Heights and Flatbush, west of the Rugby section.
Sutter Avenue-Rutland Road sits at Sutter Avenue, Rutland Road and East 98th Street, on the East Flatbush and Brownsville border.
